title: How to get more takeout orders at your restaurant
description: Get more takeout orders with better phone handling, clearer menus, tighter pickup timing, and practical marketing steps for busy restaurants.
question: How do I get more takeout orders for my restaurant without adding a lot more work?
answer: To get more takeout orders, make it easier for customers to call, place an order, and get a fast, clear pickup time. That means a clean menu, a working call path, quick phone answers, and simple reminders on your website and Google listings. An AI phone host like ROAL can help by taking pickup and delivery orders from your live menu and sending clean tickets to the kitchen.
summary: You’ll learn simple ways to bring in more takeout calls and turn more of them into confirmed orders.
intro:
More takeout orders usually come from two things: being easy to reach and being easy to order from. If people call and nobody picks up, or the menu is hard to understand, they move on.

The fix is practical. Tighten up your phone setup, make your menu clearer, and give callers a fast way to place an order. For many restaurants, an AI phone host like [ROAL](/about) can help answer the phone, take pickup orders, and send the ticket to the kitchen without adding more staff load.

sections.h2: Why are takeout calls slipping away?
sections.body:
Start by looking at the most common leak points in a takeout order path. A caller does not care about your systems. They care about whether someone answers, whether the menu is clear, and whether the pickup time makes sense.

Use this quick check on your own restaurant:
- Call your main number during lunch rush and after hours.
- See whether the phone rings too long, goes to voicemail, or gets a confusing menu.
- Check whether your website and Google listing show the same hours, address, and phone number.
- Ask your staff what callers most often ask: hours, parking, sold-out items, or menu questions.

If the same issues keep showing up, that is your opportunity. For example, if a caller asks, “Do you still have chicken parm?” and the answer is hard to find, you lose the order before it starts. ROAL can answer menu questions from the live menu, but the bigger lesson is simple: make the first five seconds of the call very easy. A good phone line is often the difference between a call that becomes a ticket and a call that disappears.

sections.h2: How do you make the phone a better sales channel?
sections.body:
Your phone should be treated like a takeout counter, not a side task. If it rings too often and nobody can get to it, you are losing direct orders that were already interested in buying.

A simple setup helps a lot:
1. Make sure the restaurant’s existing number forwards correctly.
2. Test what happens when the line is busy and when nobody answers.
3. Use one clear greeting: “Thanks for calling [restaurant name]. Would you like pickup or delivery today?”
4. Keep the order path short: items, sizes, modifiers, name, phone, and ready time.

A useful call script for staff is: “I can take that now. What size would you like, and any changes on it?” That keeps the conversation moving and reduces back-and-forth. ROAL does this from the live menu, speaks the caller’s language, and confirms the order back before sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. If you are comparing tools, [how it works](/how-it-works) is a good place to see the basic flow without the guesswork.

sections.h2: What should be on your menu, hours, and Google listings?
sections.body:
Customers call because they want an answer fast. If your menu, hours, and address are scattered or outdated, people give up and order somewhere else. The easiest wins usually come from fixing the basics first.

Make this checklist part of your weekly routine:
- Hours are the same on your website, Google listing, and voicemail greeting.
- The menu is readable on mobile.
- Popular takeout items are easy to find.
- Sold-out items are removed or marked clearly.
- Parking, entrance, and pickup instructions are easy to see.

Here is a simple example. Say you sell a $28 average takeout order. If 10 callers a week ask basic menu questions and half of them hang up because they cannot get a clear answer, that is 5 lost orders. Plug in your own numbers and look at the result. This is why [restaurant website must-haves](/blog/restaurant-website-must-haves) and the call button on your Google Maps listing matter so much. If your listings are clean, more people will call with confidence instead of bouncing to a delivery app or a competitor.

sections.h2: How do you price takeout so callers say yes?
sections.body:
A lot of restaurants lose takeout orders because the total feels unclear. People want to know the item price, any extra charge, and when it will be ready. The cleaner your answer, the easier it is to close the order.

Try this approach on every call:
- Quote the item or order clearly.
- Repeat any modifiers before confirming.
- Give one ready-time estimate, not a vague promise.
- Mention pickup details if they matter, like parking or entrance instructions.

Example script: “That comes to $28 before tax. I have it for pickup in about 20 minutes. What name should I put on the order?” That is simple, direct, and easy for a busy caller to follow.

If your restaurant takes delivery orders too, keep the payment rule clear. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment still happens at pickup or however your restaurant already handles it. That keeps the process familiar for you and your staff. For owners who want a rough cost comparison, [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) can help frame the tradeoff without guessing.

sections.h2: How can you handle busy periods without losing orders?
sections.body:
Rush periods are where takeout money slips away fastest. Lunch, Friday night, bad weather, and holidays can all stack up calls while staff are already juggling food and in-person guests.

Use a simple triage plan:
1. Decide which calls must reach a person and which can be handled by a phone host.
2. Forward the restaurant number when you are busy or unanswered.
3. Keep a clean handoff for complaints, catering, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests.
4. Review call history after the rush to see what customers asked.

Here is a practical example. If two staff members are on the line, one expediting food and one dealing with the counter, missed calls pile up. Forwarding the phone means the caller still gets an answer while your team keeps cooking. On many phones and carriers, call forwarding can be set with carrier codes or in a web portal, but codes vary, so confirm with your carrier and test with a real call. If you need a reference, [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) is a helpful starting point.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line when you go live, and you can forward all calls or just the ones that are busy or unanswered. That makes it easier to protect takeout revenue during the moments when the line gets slammed.

sections.h2: What should you measure each week to get more takeout orders?
sections.body:
You do not need a giant dashboard to improve takeout. You need a few numbers you can actually use. The goal is to spot where calls are getting lost and where good calls are becoming paid orders.

Track these items every week:
- Calls that came in during open hours.
- Calls that were answered versus missed.
- Questions you had to answer more than once.
- Orders that were confirmed and sent to the kitchen.
- Common reasons callers did not finish.

A simple table like this can help:

| Item | Example number | What to do |
|---|---:|---|
| Missed calls during dinner | 12 | Add forwarding or cover the phone |
| Menu questions | 18 | Update website, FAQs, or phone host answers |
| Confirmed pickup orders | 34 | Review what sold best |
| Orders with special notes | 9 | Make kitchen instructions clearer |

If you use an AI phone host, look at the call history, transcripts, and kitchen tickets together. ROAL includes those in the dashboard, along with menu editing and FAQs, so the owner can tighten the system over time. The point is not to admire the data. The point is to find the next fix that helps one more caller place an order.

sections.h2: Which small changes usually bring the fastest wins?
sections.body:
The quickest gains usually come from removing friction, not from big marketing plans. Independent restaurants do better when the order path is simple and the caller feels heard fast.

Start with these moves:
- Add a clear pickup line on your website and Google listing.
- Make sure hours, address, and parking are correct everywhere.
- Put top sellers near the front of the menu.
- Train staff on one short phone script.
- Use call forwarding or a phone host during rushes.

If you want one place to start, build a test host from your public menu and see how it handles the most common calls. You can [build a free test host](/try) from your website, Google Maps link, or restaurant name and city, then test-call it right in the browser. That makes it easier to hear your own menu the way a caller hears it.

One final thought: getting more takeout orders is usually not about one magic trick. It is about answering faster, quoting clearly, and making the next step obvious. Do that well, and more callers will finish the order instead of hanging up and trying somewhere else.

takeaways: Make the phone easier to answer and easier to order from.
Keep menu, hours, address, and pickup details consistent everywhere.
Use clear quotes, simple ready times, and short scripts on the phone.
Review call history weekly to find the questions and leaks that cost orders.

faq.q: How do I get more takeout orders without spending a lot on ads?
faq.a: Focus on the phone path first. Make sure calls are answered, your menu is easy to understand, and your hours and address are accurate on your website and Google listing. Those changes help turn existing local demand into confirmed orders without adding a big ad budget.

faq.q: What should I say on the phone to get more pickup orders?
faq.a: Use a short, confident script. Try: “Thanks for calling [restaurant name]. Would you like pickup or delivery today?” Then move straight to items, sizes, modifiers, name, phone number, and ready time. Short calls are easier for busy customers to finish.

faq.q: Is an AI phone host worth it for takeout orders?
faq.a: It can be, especially if your phone gets busy and calls are slipping away. ROAL answers the restaurant’s phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen. It also handles questions it can answer and passes harder calls to staff.

faq.q: How do I stop missing calls during lunch or dinner rush?
faq.a: Use call forwarding when the line is busy or unanswered, and confirm the setup with your carrier or phone system. Test it with a real call before a rush. You can also route calls to a phone host so orders keep moving while staff focus on the dining room or kitchen.
